At the top of the stairs he regained his composure and decided to let out his famous devilish laugh. He had found it extremely useful several times before. People said it had turned Lord Raker's wig grey overnight, and it had certainly made three of Lady Canterville's French governesses announce their resignations before their first month was over. So he gave his most horrible laugh, making the old vaulted ceiling echo again and again. But the terrifying sound had barely faded when a door opened and Mrs. Otis appeared in a pale blue dressing gown. 'I'm afraid you're feeling quite unwell,' she said, 'so I've brought a bottle of Dr. Dobell's medicine. If you have indigestion, it's an excellent treatment.' The ghost glared furiously at her and immediately prepared to turn into a large black dog. This was a skill for which he was rightly famous; the family doctor always blamed it for the permanent loss of reason suffered by Lord Canterville's uncle, the Hon. Thomas Horton. But approaching footsteps made him hesitate over his dreadful plan. Instead, he gave off a faint glow and disappeared with a deep, graveyard groan, just as the twins reached him.

Once in his room, he lost control completely and became terribly upset. The twins' bad manners and Mrs. Otis's stubbornly practical attitude were naturally very annoying. What truly distressed him, however, was his failure to wear the suit of armour. He had hoped even modern Americans would be stirred by the sight of a Ghost in Armour, if only out of respect for their national poet Longfellow. He himself had passed many a weary hour enjoying that poet's graceful, appealing verse while the Cantervilles were away in London. Besides, the armour belonged to him. He had worn it to great effect at the Kenilworth tournament, where the Virgin Queen herself had praised it highly. Yet when he tried putting it on now, the enormous breastplate and steel helmet proved far too heavy. He had crashed onto the stone floor, badly scraping both knees and bruising the knuckles of his right hand.

For several days afterward he was extremely ill. He barely left his room, except to keep the bloodstain in good condition. By taking excellent care of himself, however, he recovered and decided to make a third attempt to frighten the United States Minister and his family.

His intelligence and disposition, different as they were from hers, would have met every wish she entertained. Such a marriage must have benefited them both: her easy liveliness might have softened his character and improved his manners, while his discernment, learning, and experience of the world must have brought her still more substantial advantages.

But no happy alliance of this sort could now instruct an admiring public in the true nature of married bliss. A union of quite another character, which made the former impossible, would shortly take place within their family.

How Wickham and Lydia could maintain any tolerable degree of independence she could not conceive. Yet she could readily imagine how little enduring happiness awaited two people joined solely because their passions outweighed their virtue.

Mr. Gardiner soon addressed another letter to his brother. He answered Mr. Bennet's thanks briefly, assuring him of his readiness to further the happiness of any member of his family, and ending with an earnest request that the matter never be raised with him again. The chief business of the letter was to announce Mr. Wickham's determination to leave the militia.

"I was particularly anxious that he should take this step," he continued, "once his marriage had been agreed upon. I believe you will share my opinion that his departure from that corps is most desirable, for his own sake as well as my niece's. Mr. Wickham intends to enter the Regulars; and some among his old friends remain both willing and able to help him in the army. He has been promised an ensign's commission in General----'s regiment, at present stationed in the north. Its distance from this portion of the kingdom is a considerable advantage. His promises are good; and I hope that among new acquaintances, where each has a reputation to maintain, both will behave more cautiously. I have written to Colonel Forster explaining our current arrangements and asking him to reassure Mr. Wickham's several creditors in and about Brighton that they will soon receive payment, for which I have made myself responsible. Would you undertake to convey the same assurances to those he owes in Meryton? I shall append a list drawn from his account. He has declared all his debts; at least, I trust he has not misled us. Haggerston has received our instructions, and everything should be settled within a week. They will then proceed to his regiment, unless an invitation to Longbourn reaches them first. Mrs. Gardiner tells me that my niece is exceedingly eager to see you all before quitting the south.

The storm raged all night, but nothing especially remarkable happened. The next morning, though, the family came down to breakfast and found the dreadful bloodstain back on the floor. 'I don't think Paragon Detergent can be to blame,' Washington said. 'I've tested it on everything. It must be the ghost.' He cleaned away the stain for a second time, but it returned the next morning. On the third morning it was there again, although Mr. Otis himself had locked the library that night and taken the key upstairs. By now the whole family was interested. Mr. Otis began to think he had denied the existence of ghosts too firmly. Mrs. Otis announced that she intended to join the Psychical Society. Washington prepared a long letter to Mr. Myers and Mr. Podmore about why bloodstains connected with crimes would not disappear. That night, all doubts about whether ghosts actually existed were settled forever.

The day had been warm and sunny, and the whole family went for a drive in the cool evening air. They returned at nine and ate a light supper. Their conversation never turned to ghosts, so they did not even have the expectation of seeing something supernatural that so often comes before such experiences. As Mr. Otis later told me, they simply discussed the usual subjects of educated Americans from good society. These included how much better an actress Miss Fanny Davenport was than Sarah Bernhardt; how difficult it was to get fresh sweetcorn, buckwheat cakes, and hominy even in the finest English houses; Boston's importance to the development of the world's soul; the benefits of the luggage-checking system on railway journeys; and how pleasant the New York accent sounded beside the London drawl. Nothing supernatural was mentioned, and nobody referred in any way to Sir Simon de Canterville. At eleven the family went to bed, and by half past eleven every light was out. Some time later, Mr. Otis woke to an odd noise in the corridor outside his room. It sounded like metal clanking and seemed to draw closer each moment. He immediately got up, lit a match, and checked the time. It was exactly one o'clock. He remained perfectly calm and felt his pulse, which showed no sign of fever. The strange noise continued, and now he could clearly hear footsteps along with it. He slipped on his slippers, took a small, long, narrow bottle from his dressing case, and opened the door.
